topic: Contextual bandits for recommendation; off-policy evaluation (OPE) and its assumptions; sequential recommender backbones and leakage-free offline evaluation

papers.title: A Contextual-Bandit Approach to Personalized News Article Recommendation
papers.authors: Lihong Li, Wei Chu, John Langford, Robert E. Schapire
papers.summary: Frames news recommendation as a contextual bandit and proposes LinUCB (disjoint/hybrid linear payoff with ridge-regression confidence ellipsoids, choosing argmax of mean + alpha * sqrt(x^T A^-1 x)). It evaluates offline via replay on uniformly-random Yahoo! Front Page logs (over 33M events), reporting a 12.5% click lift over a context-free bandit.
papers.relevance: Canonical contextual-bandit baseline. We run LinUCB on frozen backbone (SASRec/GRU) state embeddings and item embeddings over the 500-3000 item candidate set. Unlike our setting, it is myopic (one-step reward) and does not reason about the support of offline data; its confidence width is a natural per-(s,a) uncertainty signal we can compare against offline support counts.
papers.correction_note: arXiv page confirms title, authors, WWW 2010 (DOI 10.1145/1772690.1772758), and the 12.5% lift.

papers.title: Unbiased Offline Evaluation of Contextual-bandit-based News Article Recommendation Algorithms
papers.authors: Lihong Li, Wei Chu, John Langford, Xuanhui Wang
papers.summary: Proposes the 'replay' (rejection-sampling) offline evaluator: stream logged events and keep only those where the evaluated policy picks the logged action. It is provably unbiased when the logs come from a uniformly random policy, and the paper validates it against online bucket tests on Yahoo! data.
papers.relevance: Shows why OPE needs a known, full-support logging policy. With a few thousand actions, replay keeps about 1/|A| of events, so it is only useful as a sanity check if we include a uniform-exploration slice in our simulated logs. It also motivates our choice to log with a known stochastic behavior policy.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm this is revised from the WSDM 2011 version (DOI 10.1145/1935826.1935878). The arXiv v1 is from 2010.

papers.title: Deep Bayesian Bandits Showdown: An Empirical Comparison of Bayesian Deep Networks for Thompson Sampling
papers.authors: Carlos Riquelme, George Tucker, Jasper Snoek
papers.summary: Benchmarks approximate-posterior methods (variational, dropout, bootstrap, ensembles, NeuralLinear, etc.) combined with Thompson sampling on many contextual bandit problems. It finds that methods that work well in supervised learning often underperform in sequential decision-making because their uncertainty converges slowly, while simple NeuralLinear (Bayesian linear regression on a learned last layer) is robust.
papers.relevance: Justifies a NeuralLinear-TS bandit baseline on top of our backbone: it is cheap and stable. Its finding that uncertainty estimates often adapt poorly in the online setting is directly relevant to our core method, which gates online updates on critic-ensemble uncertainty. We must check that uncertainty is calibrated against true support/error in the simulator rather than assuming it.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICLR 2018.

papers.title: Neural Contextual Bandits with UCB-based Exploration
papers.authors: Dongruo Zhou, Lihong Li, Quanquan Gu
papers.summary: NeuralUCB builds UCB confidence bounds from the neural tangent (gradient) features of a network fit to rewards, with O~(sqrt(T)) regret under an NTK-style analysis. In practice it needs a p x p (often diagonal-approximated) design matrix over network parameters.
papers.relevance: Optional neural bandit baseline. It is expensive per step (gradient per candidate item, about 3000 per state), so if we use it we will use the diagonal approximation or last-layer gradients only. Like LinUCB it is a one-step, online-exploration method and does not use offline support.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICML 2020.

papers.title: Neural Thompson Sampling
papers.authors: Weitong Zhang, Dongruo Zhou, Lihong Li, Quanquan Gu
papers.summary: A Thompson-sampling contextual bandit whose reward posterior is centered at the network output, with variance from neural tangent features. It has an O(sqrt(T)) cumulative regret bound for bounded reward functions.
papers.relevance: Alternative neural-bandit baseline with the same compute caveats as NeuralUCB. We would likely prefer NeuralLinear TS (Riquelme et al.) for speed and cite NeuralTS as the theoretically grounded variant.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICLR 2021.

papers.title: The Self-Normalized Estimator for Counterfactual Learning
papers.authors: Adith Swaminathan, Thorsten Joachims
papers.summary: Shows that learning with the unbiased IPS counterfactual risk estimator suffers from 'propensity overfitting' and proposes the self-normalized IPS (SNIPS) estimator, sum(w*r)/sum(w), which uses the weight sum as a multiplicative control variate. It is used in Norm-POEM.
papers.relevance: SNIPS is our default propensity-based OPE estimator and diagnostic. The mean weight (1/n) sum(w), which should be about 1 under full support, is a cheap check for support deficiency and propensity bugs. It requires the known behavior propensities that our simulated logs provide and real KuaiRec logs lack.
papers.correction_note: The NeurIPS proceedings page confirms the title, authors, NIPS 28 (2015), propensity overfitting, and Norm-POEM.

papers.title: Doubly Robust Policy Evaluation and Learning
papers.authors: Miroslav Dudik, John Langford, Lihong Li
papers.summary: Combines a direct reward model with IPS correction on the residual. The estimate is accurate (unbiased in the idealized case) if either the propensity model or the reward model is correct, and in practice it has lower variance than IPS and lower bias than the direct method.
papers.relevance: We report DR (and SNDR) alongside SNIPS for one-step evaluation of bandit and RL policies on simulated logs. On actions with zero behavior support, the DR correction term vanishes and DR collapses to the reward model's extrapolation, which is exactly the over-optimism our project targets.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICML 2011.

papers.title: Doubly Robust Off-policy Value Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Nan Jiang, Lihong Li
papers.summary: Extends DR to sequential decision-making using per-decision importance weights plus a learned Q/V baseline. It is unbiased and can have much lower variance than (per-decision) importance sampling. The paper also gives hardness lower bounds and a safe-policy-improvement application.
papers.relevance: This is the sequential DR estimator we use for multi-step simulated episodes, with FQE as the Q baseline. Products of per-step weights over the horizon make ESS diagnostics essential.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICML 2016.

papers.title: Batch Policy Learning under Constraints
papers.authors: Hoang M. Le, Cameron Voloshin, Yisong Yue
papers.summary: Gives a meta-algorithm for constrained batch policy learning that reduces to batch RL (FQI) and online learning subroutines. It introduces a simple OPE method with PAC-style bounds, Fitted Q Evaluation (FQE): iterative regression of Q^pi on r + gamma*Q(s', pi(s')). The abstract only says 'a simple OPE method'; the paper body (Algorithm 3, called as FQE(pi, c) inside the main algorithm) names it FQE.
papers.relevance: FQE is our propensity-free OPE estimator and the Q baseline for DR. It needs no propensities but relies on function approximation and coverage (concentrability). On low-support actions it extrapolates, so we compare FQE error against true simulator returns as a function of target-policy mass on unsupported actions.
papers.correction_note: PMLR v97 pp. 3703-3712 confirmed. I extracted the PMLR PDF text and confirmed the FQE name in the body (Algorithm 3), so the earlier caveat 'we did not re-fetch' no longer applies.

papers.title: Empirical Study of Off-Policy Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Cameron Voloshin, Hoang M. Le, Nan Jiang, Yisong Yue
papers.summary: Introduces the COBS benchmark suite and stress-tests IPS-family estimators (IS, PDIS, WIS, PDWIS), hybrid estimators (DR, WDR, MAGIC), and direct methods (FQE, Q^pi(lambda), Retrace(lambda), Tree-Backup, model-based AM, IH) across horizon, policy mismatch, stochasticity, and representation. Its guideline table (Table 15) recommends: FQE for stochastic environments with severe policy mismatch; Q(lambda) for moderate mismatch when compute is not an issue; IH for long horizons with mild mismatch; PDWIS for short horizons with mild mismatch; and hybrid MAGIC (with FQE or Q(lambda)) under severe model misspecification.
papers.relevance: Guides our OPE protocol: report several estimator families, vary the behavior/target mismatch, and score OPE against simulator ground truth. Unlike COBS, we focus on mismatch caused by low action support in a recommender action space.
papers.correction_note: Venue confirmed via the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks proceedings and neurips.cc. I corrected the summary of the guidelines: the paper recommends FQE for severe mismatch in stochastic environments, not for long horizons. For long horizons it recommends IH, and only under mild mismatch. For misspecification it recommends MAGIC specifically.

papers.title: Open Bandit Dataset and Pipeline: Towards Realistic and Reproducible Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.authors: Yuta Saito, Shunsuke Aihara, Megumi Matsutani, Yusuke Narita
papers.summary: Releases the Open Bandit Dataset (ZOZOTOWN logs from multiple policies, including uniform random, with true propensities) and the Open Bandit Pipeline (OBP), a Python library implementing IPS/SNIPS/DR/SNDR/switch/DRos and others, with an evaluation-of-OPE protocol.
papers.relevance: We can use OBP's estimator implementations to avoid bugs and follow its evaluation-of-OPE protocol (relative error versus on-policy ground truth). Like OBD, our simulated logs carry true propensities. Unlike OBD, our state is a sequence and our policies are multi-step.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm the NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks Track.

papers.title: Off-policy Bandits with Deficient Support
papers.authors: Noveen Sachdeva, Yi Su, Thorsten Joachims
papers.summary: Shows that IPS-based off-policy learning can fail catastrophically when the logging policy lacks full support (common in large action spaces). It studies three remedies: restricting the action space, reward extrapolation, and restricting the policy space. The conclusion finds restricting the policy space 'particularly effective': it gives explicit risk control, learns well, and is easy to implement.
papers.relevance: This is the closest bandit-side antecedent to our support-aware idea. Our method extends 'restrict policy shift on low-support actions' to sequential offline-to-online fine-tuning, with support estimated per (state, action). We must cite it and position against it in any novelty claim.
papers.correction_note: KDD '20 confirmed (DOI 10.1145/3394486.3403139). The 'policy-space restriction works best' claim is confirmed from the paper's Conclusions section (via Cornell PDF text).

papers.title: Session-based Recommendations with Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.authors: Balazs Hidasi, Alexandros Karatzoglou, Linas Baltrunas, Domonkos Tikk
papers.summary: GRU4Rec models sessions with a GRU over item sequences, trained with session-parallel mini-batches, in-batch negative sampling, and ranking losses (BPR, TOP1). It beats item-kNN on two session datasets.
papers.relevance: This is a cheap backbone and state encoder (GRU state is a natural RL state). It serves as a supervised-ranker baseline and an ablation versus SASRec.
papers.correction_note: arXiv page/DBLP confirms ICLR 2016.

papers.title: Personalized Top-N Sequential Recommendation via Convolutional Sequence Embedding
papers.authors: Jiaxi Tang, Ke Wang
papers.summary: Caser embeds the last L items as an 'image' and applies horizontal and vertical convolutions to capture union-level and point-level sequential patterns, combined with a user embedding.
papers.relevance: We cite it for completeness but likely do not run it. It is usually weaker than SASRec, and its user embedding hurts generalization to the cold or limited-history states that arise in the simulator.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm WSDM 2018.

papers.title: Self-Attentive Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Wang-Cheng Kang, Julian McAuley
papers.summary: SASRec is a causal (left-to-right) Transformer over item sequences that predicts the next item. It outperforms MC/CNN/RNN baselines while being about an order of magnitude more efficient. It was originally trained with BCE and one sampled negative per positive.
papers.relevance: This is our primary supervised ranker and shared state encoder for BC, bandit, and RL heads. Its causal masking matches the RL state definition (history up to t) and avoids future leakage within a sequence.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm ICDM 2018.

papers.title: BERT4Rec: Sequential Recommendation with Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformer
papers.authors: Fei Sun, Jun Liu, Jian Wu, Changhua Pei, Xiao Lin, Wenwu Ou, Peng Jiang
papers.summary: A bidirectional Transformer trained with a Cloze (masked-item) objective and full softmax. It reports gains over SASRec and GRU4Rec on four datasets.
papers.relevance: This is a candidate backbone that we expect not to adopt. Bidirectional training does not match the causal state used by RL, and later work attributes most of its gain to the loss (see Klenitskiy & Vasilev 2023).
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm CIKM 2019 and four datasets.

papers.title: Turning Dross Into Gold Loss: is BERT4Rec really better than SASRec?
papers.authors: Anton Klenitskiy, Alexey Vasilev
papers.summary: Shows that BERT4Rec's reported advantage over SASRec is largely due to its full softmax cross-entropy loss. SASRec trained with full CE beats BERT4Rec in both quality and training speed, and with sampled negatives it needs many more than one negative.
papers.relevance: This directly supports our backbone choice: SASRec with full softmax CE over the 500-3000 item candidate set, which is cheap at this catalog size. It also means the BC policy and the supervised ranker can share the same softmax head.
papers.correction_note: The arXiv page lists DOI 10.1145/3604915.3610644 (RecSys '23 proceedings). The abstract claims match.

papers.title: A Critical Study on Data Leakage in Recommender System Offline Evaluation
papers.authors: Yitong Ji, Aixin Sun, Jie Zhang, Chenliang Li
papers.summary: Shows that splits ignoring the global timeline (e.g., leave-last-one-out) let models train on interactions occurring after test events. With BPR, NeuMF, SASRec, and LightGCN on MovieLens-25M, Yelp, and Amazon data, models recommend future items, and leakage changes model rankings. The paper proposes a timeline-based evaluation scheme.
papers.relevance: This mandates our global temporal split on KuaiRec's big matrix timestamps for all supervised-ranker results and for building the simulator/user-state encoder.
papers.correction_note: Journal reference confirmed: ACM Trans. Inf. Syst. 41(3), 75:1-75:27 (2023).

papers.title: Take a Fresh Look at Recommender Systems from an Evaluation Standpoint
papers.authors: Aixin Sun
papers.summary: Argues that random and leave-one-out splits ignore the global timeline, causing data leakage and making the popularity baseline ill-defined. It advocates evaluation that respects the global timeline and decision context.
papers.relevance: Our popularity baseline will be computed only from interactions before the cutoff (or a recent window before each test time), following this paper's definition issue.
papers.correction_note: arXiv confirms SIGIR 2023 Perspectives Paper Track (DOI 10.1145/3539618.3591931).

papers.title: Are We Evaluating Rigorously? Benchmarking Recommendation for Reproducible Evaluation and Fair Comparison
papers.authors: Zhu Sun, Di Yu, Hui Fang, Jie Yang, Xinghua Qu, Jie Zhang, Cong Geng
papers.summary: Reviews 85 papers to identify evaluation factors (splitting, sampling, tuning, metrics). It shows these factors materially change results and releases daisyRec, which benchmarks seven well-tuned methods on six datasets and six metrics for implicit-feedback top-N recommendation.
papers.relevance: We use it as a checklist for our evaluation protocol: equal tuning budgets per baseline, reporting of split and negative-sampling choices, and multiple seeds.
papers.correction_note: The ACM DL returned 403. I confirmed the authors, RecSys 2020 pp. 23-32, the DOI, and the 85-paper review on the TU Delft research portal page (and the Macquarie record via search). The DOI resolves (302) to dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3383313.3412489.

papers.title: On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation
papers.authors: Walid Krichene, Steffen Rendle
papers.summary: Proves and shows empirically that sampled metrics (ranking the target among a few random negatives) are inconsistent with exact metrics and can reverse model comparisons. At small sample sizes they collapse toward AUC. Corrections exist, but sampling should be avoided.
papers.relevance: With at most about 3000 candidates we compute full-ranking HR/Recall@K, NDCG@K, and MRR exactly. If we report sampled metrics for comparison with prior work, we label them clearly as secondary.
papers.correction_note: The Google Research page confirms the title, authors, and KDD 2020. The Best Paper (research track) award is confirmed by the SIGKDD award announcement coverage (insidehpc, syncedreview), not by the Google page.

papers.title: Exploring Data Splitting Strategies for the Evaluation of Recommendation Models
papers.authors: Zaiqiao Meng, Richard McCreadie, Craig Macdonald, Iadh Ounis
papers.summary: Surveys the split strategies used in 17 recent papers, then compares three of them experimentally: leave-one-last item, leave-one-last basket, and global temporal split. The comparison covers seven models (NMF, BPR, NeuMF, VAECF, NGCF, Triple2vec, VBCAR) on two grocery datasets (Tafeng, Dunnhumby). The split substantially changes model rankings. The paper also notes that leave-one-last and user-based temporal splits leak future interactions into training.
papers.relevance: Supports reporting our split explicitly and choosing a global temporal split. As a robustness check, we may show that leave-one-out changes baseline rankings on KuaiRec.
papers.correction_note: Venue and DOI confirmed via the Glasgow eprints record (the arXiv PDF carries a template DOI). Correction: the three strategies compared are leave-one-last item, leave-one-last basket, and global temporal. Random split was not among them, and user-based temporal was excluded as near-identical to leave-one-last item. Both datasets are grocery/basket data.

papers.title: KuaiRec: A Fully-observed Dataset and Insights for Evaluating Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Chongming Gao, Shijun Li, Wenqiang Lei, Jiawei Chen, Biao Li, Peng Jiang, Xiangnan He, Jiaxin Mao, Tat-Seng Chua
papers.summary: Releases KuaiRec with a nearly fully observed 1411 x 3327 user-item matrix plus a sparse big matrix from Kuaishou. Using it, the paper shows that data density and exposure bias change the ranking of methods, and that imputing missing interactions for user simulation helps only in some cases. The case study is on evaluating multi-round conversational recommendation.
papers.relevance: This is our data source. The fully observed small matrix gives near-ground-truth rewards for the simulator and makes on-policy ground truth available to score OPE estimators. The paper's caveat about simulation fidelity is why we label policy results as simulated.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments confirm CIKM '22 (DOI 10.1145/3511808.3557220) and 1,411 users x 3,327 items. Minor clarification added: the method-ranking insights come from a multi-round conversational recommendation case study.

claims_in_notes_disputed: voloshin2021empirical summary: the claim that 'direct methods such as FQE are often best under large mismatch or long horizons' misattributes the guidelines. Table 15 recommends FQE for stochastic environments with severe policy mismatch, IH (not FQE) for long horizons with only mild mismatch, PDWIS for short horizons with mild mismatch, and MAGIC (a specific hybrid) for severe model misspecification.

meng2020splitting summary: the claim that the paper compares 'random, leave-one-last, temporal' splits is wrong. The three strategies compared are leave-one-last item, leave-one-last basket, and global temporal split. Random split is not one of them, and the datasets are grocery (Tafeng, Dunnhumby).

topic_notes section 1: scoring OPE by 'rank correlation across candidate policies, and regret@1, following Voloshin et al. 2021' is loosely attributed. Rank correlation and regret@k come from Fu et al. 2021 (Benchmarks for Deep Off-Policy Evaluation, ICLR 2021). Voloshin et al. use relative MSE and near-top frequency, and OBP uses relative estimation error. Fu et al. 2021 is cited in the notes but missing from the paper list.
le2019fqe: the earlier caveat that the FQE name was not verified is now resolved. The PMLR PDF body names it FQE (Algorithm 3). Not an error, but the hedge should be removed.
gao2022kuairec summary: the method-ranking and imputation insights are specific to a multi-round conversational recommendation case study, not to general recommendation. This is a minor scope issue.
topic_notes:
1) OPE validity, assumptions, and diagnostics. Propensity-based estimators are valid only with KNOWN (or well-estimated) behavior propensities pi_b(a|s) and COVERAGE (overlap/absolute continuity): pi_e(a|s)>0 => pi_b(a|s)>0. These are IPS, SNIPS (Swaminathan & Joachims 2015), DR and SNDR (Dudik et al. 2011), replay (Li et al. 2011, whose unbiasedness guarantee assumes uniformly random logging), and in the sequential case per-decision IS/WIS and sequential DR (Jiang & Li 2016). If coverage fails, IPS is biased by the target-policy value mass on unsupported actions, and off-policy learning can fail catastrophically (Sachdeva et al. 2020, who find that restricting the policy space is the most effective remedy). DR then silently falls back to the reward model on those actions. Direct methods (DM, FQE from Le et al. 2019, Algorithm 3) need no propensities but require realizability/completeness and concentrability, a coverage condition in distribution form. They extrapolate on low-support (s,a) pairs, which is exactly the over-optimism we study. Real KuaiRec logs have no propensities, so we will report no propensity-based OPE on real logs. All OPE runs on simulator logs generated by a known stochastic behavior policy (e.g., softmax over a popularity/ranker score with epsilon-uniform mixing, so that every action has pi_b >= epsilon/|A| unless we deliberately create support holes as a controlled factor). We report the following diagnostics for every estimator, target policy, and dataset:
- Kish ESS = (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 and ESS/n.
- Max weight, its share of the total weight, and the p99 weight.
- Mean weight (about 1 under full support; under deficient support its expectation is 1 minus the unsupported mass, so deviations flag support or propensity problems).
- Clipping rate if clipped estimators are used.
- 'Unsupported mass' = E_s[sum_a pi_e(a|s) 1{pi_b(a|s) < tau}].
- For multi-step OPE: per-step ESS of cumulative weights.
- Bootstrap CIs over seeds.
Because the simulator gives on-policy ground truth, we score each OPE method by relative error and RMSE (as in Voloshin et al. 2021 and OBP's relative-estimation-error protocol), and by rank correlation across candidate policies and regret@1 (as in Fu et al. 2021, 'Benchmarks for Deep Off-Policy Evaluation', ICLR 2021, which should be added to the paper list). Following Voloshin et al.'s guidelines, expect FQE to do well under severe mismatch in stochastic settings, hybrid MAGIC/DR-style estimators to help under model misspecification, and IS-family estimators to work only for short horizons with mild mismatch. We then plot OPE error against unsupported mass. That plot directly links OPE failure to the support question.

2) Backbone. For KuaiRec-sized data (big matrix of about 7k users and about 10.7k items; we restrict to the 500-3000 item candidate set), SASRec with full softmax cross-entropy over the candidate set is the most reasonable choice. It is fast, strong, and causal (Kang & McAuley 2018), and Klenitskiy & Vasilev (2023) show that full-CE SASRec beats BERT4Rec in quality and speed. BERT4Rec's bidirectional Cloze training does not match the causal 'history up to t' state that RL uses. GRU4Rec is the cheap ablation and alternative encoder. Caser is optional. A single SASRec encoder can be shared: the supervised ranker, BC (the same softmax), and the state for the bandits (LinUCB / NeuralLinear-TS on frozen embeddings) and the offline/online RL Q-heads. Riquelme et al. (2018) suggest NeuralLinear as a robust TS baseline. NeuralUCB/NeuralTS are optional because per-candidate gradient features over about 3000 items are costly.

3) Leakage-free split. Use a GLOBAL temporal split on big-matrix timestamps (Ji et al. 2023; Sun 2023; Meng et al. 2020, who compared leave-one-last item/basket against global temporal splits and noted that leave-one-last and user-based temporal splits leak future interactions). Pick cut times T_val < T_test. Training uses only events before T_val, validation uses [T_val, T_test), and test uses events at or after T_test. Test-time user states contain only that user's events before the predicted event. All of the following are fit on pre-cutoff data only: item vocabulary, popularity counts, normalizations (e.g., the watch_ratio threshold or clipping), and hyperparameter search. Do not use leave-one-out or random splits except as an explicitly labeled robustness check. Keep the simulator reward model (from the small matrix) separate from the ranker's evaluation data. Check user/item overlap between the small and big matrices, and exclude small-matrix (user,item) pairs used as ground truth from any training data the ranker sees.

4) Metrics. With at most about 3000 candidates, full ranking is cheap. Report exact full-ranking HR/Recall@{10,20}, NDCG@{10,20}, and MRR (Krichene & Rendle 2020 show sampled metrics are inconsistent), with mean ± std over at least 3 seeds and the same tuning budget for every method (Sun et al. 2020). Report sampled metrics (e.g., 1 positive + 100 negatives) only as labeled secondary numbers for comparability, if at all. For policies, the primary metric is the simulator's on-policy return (cumulative watch_ratio-based reward over an episode). Report it together with support statistics of the learned policy: unsupported mass, the distribution of behavior-policy support counts of chosen actions, and catalog coverage/diversity.

topic: Offline RL algorithms for discrete action spaces and how well they suit large discrete action spaces (hundreds to thousands of items)

papers.title: Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Aviral Kumar, Aurick Zhou, George Tucker, Sergey Levine
papers.summary: Adds a regularizer to the Bellman error so the learned Q-function lower-bounds the policy's value: it pushes Q down on actions from a maximizing distribution and up on dataset actions. In the discrete CQL(H) variant this is alpha*(logsumexp_a Q(s,a) - Q(s,a_data)). The Atari experiments built it on QR-DQN.
papers.relevance: Our primary discrete offline RL baseline. Over 500-3000 items, logsumexp over a full Q-head is cheap and exact. Its single global alpha is what support-aware fine-tuning replaces with per-(s,a) conservatism tied to support or uncertainty. The official code (aviralkumar2907/CQL, atari/ folder, on top of batch_rl QR-DQN) and d3rlpy DiscreteCQL are the reproduction sources.
papers.correction_note: arXiv abs page confirms title and authors. NeurIPS 2020 (NeurIPS 33) confirmed on the proceedings.neurips.cc abstract page.

papers.title: Benchmarking Batch Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
papers.authors: Scott Fujimoto, Edoardo Conti, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Joelle Pineau
papers.summary: Benchmarks off-policy and batch deep RL on Atari with data from a single partially trained behavior policy. Many methods, including REM and QR-DQN, underperform both online DQN and the behavior policy itself. The paper introduces discrete BCQ, which trains a behavior-cloning network G_omega and restricts the greedy argmax to actions whose relative behavior probability G(a|s)/max G exceeds a threshold tau.
papers.relevance: The required second baseline and the closest prior work to 'restrict policy shift on low-support actions'. Our novelty claim has to separate support-aware fine-tuning from discrete BCQ's hard behavior-probability filter. Its single-behavior-policy data regime is also the 'narrow logs' regime we study. Code: sfujim/BCQ discrete_BCQ/, and d3rlpy DiscreteBCQ (action_flexibility=0.3).
papers.correction_note: The arXiv comments field reads 'Deep RL Workshop, NeurIPS 2019'. The abstract confirms single partially trained behavior policy, underperformance versus online DQN and the behavior policy, and the discrete BCQ adaptation.

papers.title: Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration
papers.authors: Scott Fujimoto, David Meger, Doina Precup
papers.summary: Identifies extrapolation error as the reason off-policy RL fails on fixed batches. Proposes batch-constrained RL (continuous BCQ), which uses a generative model with a perturbation network to keep actions near the data.
papers.relevance: Source of the extrapolation-error argument that motivates our research question. We use only the discrete descendant, so this paper is cited for motivation and not run.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments field reads 'ICML 2019'.

papers.title: An Optimistic Perspective on Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Rishabh Agarwal, Dale Schuurmans, Mohammad Norouzi
papers.summary: Shows that on the large, diverse DQN-Replay Atari dataset, plain off-policy agents can beat the online DQN that produced the data. Proposes Random Ensemble Mixture (REM), which enforces Bellman consistency on random convex combinations of multi-head Q estimates. Dataset size and diversity matter a lot.
papers.relevance: A non-conservative ensemble baseline, plus a ready-made Q-ensemble whose head disagreement we can test as an uncertainty signal for gating. Its success depends on diverse data, so we expect it to be over-optimistic under narrow behavior policies, which is a direct test of our hypothesis. Code: google-research/batch_rl (Dopamine/TF, multi_head_dqn + rem.gin), with a JAX port in Dopamine labs/offline_rl.
papers.correction_note: arXiv lists ICML 2020, PMLR 119:104-114. The arXiv version was first titled 'Striving for Simplicity in Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning' (v1, 2019).

papers.title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning
papers.authors: Ilya Kostrikov, Ashvin Nair, Sergey Levine
papers.summary: Never queries out-of-dataset actions. It fits V(s) as an upper expectile of Q(s,a) over dataset actions, trains Q with r+gamma V(s'), and extracts the policy by advantage-weighted behavior cloning. It also shows strong offline-to-online fine-tuning.
papers.relevance: Applies directly to discrete actions, with a categorical softmax policy in the AWR extraction step. TorchRL ships DiscreteIQLLoss (confirmed in the TorchRL 0.4 and 0.5 docs). It is the strongest 'in-sample' alternative for the offline-to-online phase and a natural backbone if CQL's underestimation hurts fine-tuning.

claims_in_notes_disputed: DISCRETE CQL LOSS section writes the TD term as 1/2*E[(Q-y)^2] and labels it 'the version used by d3rlpy'. d3rlpy DiscreteCQL defines the loss as alpha*(logsumexp - E_D Q) + L_DoubleDQN, and its discrete Q-function compute_error uses compute_huber_loss, so the d3rlpy TD term is a Huber loss, not 1/2 squared error. The penalty term and Double-DQN target are correct.

Kumar et al. (ICLR 2022) summary said 'offline RL can beat BC even when BC is trained on expert data'. The abstract's actual claim is narrower: offline RL trained on sufficiently noisy, suboptimal data can outperform BC trained on expert data, especially on long-horizon problems. Failure mode (5), 'little gain over BC when data is near-expert and narrow', is an extrapolation and not a stated result. The paper's conditions favoring offline RL are sparse rewards, long horizons and noisy data, and it argues offline RL can still beat BC on expert data in some settings. That item is reworded as our inference.

DiscreteBCQ: 'tau = 1 recovers BC' holds only loosely. With the strict '>' filter, tau -> 1 leaves only the argmax of G_omega, so the policy becomes greedy imitation (mode of G), not stochastic BC. This is a minor wording issue, not a misattribution.

Minor: the IQL entry said OpenReview could not be fetched and the DT entry said its venue came from common knowledge. Both venues are now confirmed (IQL: OpenReview 68n2s9ZJWF8 / ICLR 2022; DT: NeurIPS 2021 proceedings page), so those caveats are removed. Katakomba is now verified by a direct arXiv fetch.
topic_notes:
PRIMARY BASELINE. Use discrete CQL as the main discrete offline RL baseline, with discrete BCQ as a required second baseline. Discrete IQL is the backbone to try if CQL fine-tunes poorly.

Reasons to make CQL primary:
(i) It has a native, exact discrete objective. For 500-3000 items, logsumexp over a full Q-head costs O(|A|) per state, which is trivial on a GPU.
(ii) It is the most-cited conservative method and has official discrete code (aviralkumar2907/CQL atari/, built on batch_rl QR-DQN) plus d3rlpy DiscreteCQL.
(iii) Its single scalar alpha is the exact object our method generalizes into alpha(s,a) = g(support or uncertainty). That makes 'CQL with global alpha' the cleanest ablation.

BCQ is still mandatory because it already restricts the policy on low-support actions, so reviewers will ask how we differ from it. A further advantage: we know pi_beta, so BCQ's learned G_omega can be swapped for the true propensity to get an oracle-support ablation.

DISCRETE CQL LOSS (CQL(H)):
L(theta) = alpha * E_{s~D}[ log sum_a exp Q_theta(s,a) - E_{a~D(.|s)} Q_theta(s,a) ] + L_TD(theta)
with the Double-DQN target y = r + gamma * Q_target(s', argmax_a' Q_theta(s',a')). In d3rlpy DiscreteCQL (default alpha = 1.0, DoubleDQN base), L_TD is a Huber loss on (Q_theta(s,a) - y), not 1/2 squared error. The original Atari code used QR-DQN distributional targets instead. Report which TD loss we use.

The penalty gradient with respect to Q(s,.) is alpha * (softmax(Q(s,.)) - onehot(a_data)). It pushes down whichever items currently have high Q, whether or not they are supported, and pushes up the logged item.

DISCRETE BCQ (Fujimoto, Conti, Ghavamzadeh, Pineau 2019, NeurIPS 2019 Deep RL Workshop):
- Train G_omega(a|s) by cross-entropy on D.
- Action filter: pi(s) = argmax over {a : G_omega(a|s) / max_a' G_omega(a'|s) > tau} of Q_theta(s,a). The paper and d3rlpy default to tau = 0.3.
- Target: y = r + gamma * Q_target(s', pi(s')), Double-DQN style, with Huber loss. d3rlpy also adds an imitator logit regularizer, beta (default 0.5).
- tau = 0 recovers DQN. As tau -> 1, only the mode of G_omega survives, which gives greedy imitation (a BC-like policy).

IQL ON DISCRETE ACTIONS. IQL (ICLR 2022) applies unchanged:
- V loss: E_D[ L2^tau(Q_target(s,a) - V(s)) ] with expectile tau (around 0.7-0.9).
- Q loss: (Q(s,a) - r - gamma V(s'))^2.
- Policy: a categorical softmax pi trained by max E_D[ exp(beta * (Q - V)) * log pi(a|s) ].
Its critic never queries unlogged items, so it is attractive for offline-to-online. TorchRL provides DiscreteIQLLoss, documented in TorchRL 0.4/0.5 (default value loss smooth_l1, num_qvalue_nets = 2).

OTHER METHODS:
- Port directly to categorical policies: REM, CRR, AWAC, AWR, BRAC (exact KL to a known pi_beta), SAC-N (via discrete SAC with N critics), PBRL (OOD actions can be enumerated).
- Continuous-only as published: TD3+BC (deterministic actor with an MSE-to-action term), Fisher-BRC's gradient penalty and EDAC's diversity loss (both use action gradients). Fisher-BRC's 'Q = log pi_beta + offset' parameterization does transfer.
- Decision Transformer (NeurIPS 2021) works with a softmax over items but cannot stitch trajectories and conditions on returns that a stochastic simulated user makes unreliable. It is an optional sequence-model baseline next to SASRec.

LARGE ACTION SPACES. Wolpertinger-style approximate nearest-neighbor selection and combinatorial methods (factored Q from Tang et al. NeurIPS 2022, BraVE, SPIN at ICLR 2026) target action spaces of 10^4 to 10^6 or more, or combinatorial ones. At our scale, full enumeration is fine.

The real issue is statistical, not computational. Per-item support is extremely sparse, and embedding-shared Q heads (Q = f(s)^T e_a) spread optimism to unlogged but similar items. Gu et al. (ICML 2022) and VPQ (SIGIR 2022 short paper) are the recsys-relevant prior art. VPQ in particular already uses ensemble-variance (uncertainty-aware) weights on the Q regression target for offline sequential recommendation, so our novelty must lie in the offline-to-online phase: support-modulated update strength and online replay mixing, under known propensities.

FAILURE MODES WITH NARROW BEHAVIOR DATA:
(1) Non-conservative methods (DQN, REM, QR-DQN) overestimate unlogged items. Fujimoto et al. 2019 show that many such methods underperform both online DQN and the behavior policy on single-policy data, while REM's success relied on diverse DQN-Replay data.
(2) CQL with a global alpha is either too weak in low-support states or collapses to BC everywhere. The logsumexp term lies between max_a Q and max_a Q + log|A|, so its scale grows with log|A| and alpha does not transfer across catalog sizes. The learned Q is systematically underestimated, which causes the well-known performance dip when online fine-tuning starts. Cal-QL, in CORL, targets this.
(3) BCQ's filter measures relative behavior probability, not sample count. A near-deterministic pi_beta collapses BCQ to BC, while a diffuse pi_beta over thousands of items lets many items through, each seen almost never. G_omega errors in rarely visited states compound this.
(4) IQL and AWR extraction cannot put mass on good unlogged items, so improvement is capped by support. Large beta also gives high-variance weights.
(5) Kumar et al. (ICLR 2022) show that offline RL beats BC mainly with sparse rewards, long horizons and noisy or suboptimal data; offline RL on noisy data can even beat BC on expert data. Our inference, not a stated result of the paper: with near-deterministic, narrow behavior data, the expected gain of CQL over BC is small.
We should sweep behavior-policy temperature (data diversity) as a primary experimental axis.

REPRODUCTION SOURCES:
- d3rlpy (JMLR 23(315), 2022): DiscreteCQL, DiscreteBCQ, DiscreteSAC, DiscreteBC, NFQ, DQN, DoubleDQN.
- sfujim/BCQ discrete_BCQ/.
- aviralkumar2907/CQL atari/.
- google-research/batch_rl (REM, Dopamine/TF; JAX version in Dopamine labs/offline_rl).
- CORL (NeurIPS 2023 D&B): continuous IQL, AWAC, Cal-QL and EDAC, plus offline-to-online protocols. It has no discrete algorithms; its README points to Katakomba (NeurIPS 2023 D&B) for discrete control.
- TorchRL DiscreteIQLLoss (TorchRL docs 0.4/0.5).

papers.title: Alleviating Matthew Effect of Offline Reinforcement Learning in Interactive Recommendation
papers.authors: Chongming Gao, Kexin Huang, Jiawei Chen, Yuan Zhang, Biao Li, Peng Jiang, Shiqi Wang, Zhong Zhang, Xiangnan He
papers.summary: Shows that MOPO-style uncertainty pessimism amplifies the Matthew effect, so popular categories get over-recommended. DORL fixes this with reward r~ = r^ - lambda1*P_U + lambda2*P_E. P_U is the maximum variance over an ensemble of Gaussian DeepFM reward models, covering epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. P_E = -KL(pi_beta(.|s) || uniform) = H(pi_beta(.|s)) - log|A|, a state-only term from the estimated logging policy, whose entropy is estimated from k-order subsequence counts. The term relaxes pessimism where logging was diverse. Environment: stop when more than M same-category items appear in the last N rounds (M=0, N=4 main; RQ3 fixes M=10 and varies N). No repeated items, max 30 rounds, and reward = normalized viewing time on KuaiRec (is_click on KuaiRand-Pure). Each evaluation runs 100 trajectories after every epoch over 200 epochs. Metrics are cumulative reward, length, single-round reward, and majority-category domination (MCD).

Our differences: (1) the behavior policy is known, so support and propensity are exact rather than estimated; (2) support conservatism is per state-action rather than a state-level entropy bonus; (3) we study a limited online fine-tuning budget, which DORL does not; (4) we validate the simulator explicitly. DORL is a required baseline, and its quit rule and metrics are our default protocol.

Its user-model overestimation finding motivates our simulator-validity checks.

claims_in_notes_disputed: 'KuaiSim validates only with held-out click AUC' is overstated. KuaiSim (Table 6) reports click AUC on an 8:2 split plus policy-level depth and total reward of a DDPG agent in each rebuilt simulator. It also checks that return times fit a geometric distribution and runs sensitivity analyses. What it lacks is calibration and support-stratified error, so the criticism should be narrowed to that.

DORL's P_E is described as 'the entropy of the estimated logging policy'. The paper defines it as -KL(pi_beta(.|s) || uniform) = H(pi_beta(.|s)) - log|A|. That equals entropy only up to a constant, is a state-only term, and is estimated from k-order subsequence counts. P_U is the max variance over Gaussian ensemble members, covering both epistemic and aleatoric variance, not just ensemble disagreement.

'The convention starts with CIRS KuaiEnv and is reused by DORL'. DORL uses an equivalent KuaiRec environment (big matrix for training, small matrix for testing, category-based quit) but does not call it KuaiEnv. The protocols also differ: CIRS uses N=1, nQ=1 and max length 100 (30 in the limited-rounds setting), while DORL uses M=0, N=4, max 30, and no repeats.

CIRS's quit rule is stated in the paper as items sharing 'at least one attribute' with the current recommendation, not strictly the same category. For KuaiRec, attributes are video tags or categories.

Venue and year details: KuaiSim is NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks (confirmed), not just an arXiv preprint. Virtual-Taobao is AAAI 2019 (confirmed), not 2018. Deffayet et al. is SIGIR Forum Dec 2022 (year 2022). The Chen et al. offline-RL survey is ACM TOIS 2024 (confirmed via OpenAlex).
topic_notes:
How prior work builds environments from KuaiRec. CIRS (TOIS 2023) introduced the 'KuaiEnv' environment. DORL (SIGIR 2023) uses an equivalent KuaiRec environment without that name, and EasyRL4Rec (SIGIR 2024) packages KuaiRec and KuaiRand environments. A DeepFM user model is fit on the sparse big matrix (DORL Table 1 training split: 7,176 users, 10,728 items, 12,530,806 interactions, 31 categories). The policy is then scored on the fully observed small matrix (1,411 x 3,327, 4,676,570 interactions, about 99.6% dense; we derived the density from DORL's table, and the paper does not state it). On KuaiRec the reward is watch_ratio (play time divided by video duration), which DORL calls 'normalized viewing time'. On KuaiRand-Pure, DORL uses is_click.

The small matrix is not available during training. In DORL, training uses big-matrix logs and the learned (DeepFM ensemble) reward model, and evaluation reads the true small-matrix value.

Termination rules:
- **CIRS:** the user quits if more than nQ of the last N recommended items share at least one attribute (category) with the current item. Overall experiments use N=1, nQ=1 with max length 100; the limited-rounds setting uses 30. VirtualTaobao instead uses a distance threshold dQ.
- **DORL:** the user quits when more than M same-category items appear in the last N rounds. Main results use M=0, N=4; RQ3 fixes M=10 and varies N. No item may repeat, and episodes are capped at 30 rounds.
- **EasyRL4Rec:** exposes this as evaluation modes. FreeB allows repeats with quit on; NX_0 bans repeats with quit on; NX_X bans repeats and runs a fixed X rounds with no quit. Max length is 30.
- **KuaiSim:** gives each user a 'temper' budget, initialized to the max session length, that falls by the immediate reward each step. The user leaves when it reaches a threshold.

Candidate-set size: we saw nothing beyond 'all items in the evaluation matrix' (3,327 for KuaiRec), though we did not exhaustively check every appendix. Our 500-3000 subset is our own design choice and should be justified, for example as the top-K items by big-matrix coverage.

Standard metrics (DORL) are cumulative reward, trajectory length, and single-round reward. They are computed over 100 evaluation trajectories after each training epoch (200 epochs in DORL), plus diversity or Matthew-effect metrics such as DORL's majority-category domination (MCD).

Known criticisms:
1. **No real long-term dynamics.** Lee et al. (SIGIR 2022) found that on review-based benchmarks a greedy policy beats RL and weighting long-term reward more hurts, so long-horizon gains can be artifacts. In KuaiEnv-style environments the main long-term coupling is the hand-written quit rule. Our interpretation, not a claim from those papers, is that RL 'wins' largely by learning to diversify categories.
2. **Learned user models overestimate rewards.** EasyRL4Rec shows that user models trained with zero or few negatives predict higher rewards while true rewards are low. Policies exploit such errors: Virtual-Taobao needed an action-norm constraint, and DORL shows that ensemble-uncertainty pessimism instead amplifies popularity (Matthew) bias.
3. **Static ground truth.** The small matrix holds one watch_ratio per (user, item), with no context or order effects.
4. **Weak validation.** Rule-based simulators (RecSim, RecoGym) are not fit to data. KuaiSim's fidelity evidence is held-out click AUC (0.7234 vs. 0.6866 for the best rebuilt baseline), policy-level depth and reward comparisons, and a geometric fit of return times. It reports no calibration or support-stratified error.
5. **Next-item metrics hide offline RL failures** (Deffayet et al., SIGIR Forum 2022).
6. **Simulation studies lack shared empirical standards** (Winecoff et al.).

A careful simulator validation should check:
- **Disjoint fitting and scoring data.** Big- and small-matrix users overlap, so check interaction-level leakage explicitly.
- **Held-out prediction error:** RMSE/MAE on watch_ratio, and AUC on a thresholded 'like' proxy, using small-matrix entries never used for fitting.
- **Calibration:** reliability curves and ECE of predicted vs. true watch_ratio, plus calibration of ensemble variance (does predicted std track absolute error?).
- **Error stratified by support,** meaning behavior-policy propensity or log-count bins. This links directly to our research question.
- **Coverage:** the fraction of the candidate set, and of (user, category) cells, with adequate log support.
- **Policy-level check:** the gap between return predicted by the learned model and true small-matrix return for each policy. A large positive gap is direct evidence of simulator exploitation.
- **Long-horizon sanity:** a greedy oracle on true rewards, random, and popularity as reference points, plus a test that discounting matters (Lee et al.).
- **Sensitivity** of conclusions to quit-rule parameters (M, N), reward clipping (watch_ratio can exceed 1), and seeds.

Labeling simulated returns. Report them as 'simulated return in environment X' and name the environment version, reward definition, quit rule, horizon, and candidate set. Never call them engagement or retention. Keep three numbers separate: (a) return under the learned training simulator, (b) return under small-matrix ground truth, and (c) normalized score = (R - R_random) / (R_greedy-oracle - R_random). Use multiple seeds with confidence intervals, and state that the ground truth is static and has no real user feedback loop.

How we differ from DORL and EasyRL4Rec:
1. **Known behavior policy.** DORL and EasyRL4Rec train on real logs with unknown propensity; DORL estimates the logging policy's entropy (as -KL to uniform) from subsequence counts. We generate logs with a known behavior policy, so per-(state, action) support is exact and controllable. We can sweep coverage as an independent variable, for example through the behavior policy's temperature or a top-k restriction.
2. **Offline-to-online fine-tuning.** Neither prior work studies fine-tuning with a limited simulated online budget. We ask when online interaction helps and when it hurts, as a function of support and budget.
3. **Granularity of conservatism.** DORL's P_E is a state-level term, while its P_U is per (state, action) through ensemble variance. We use per-action support (exact, from the known behavior policy) or uncertainty to modulate update strength during fine-tuning.
4. **Explicit validation.** We separate the training simulator from the evaluation ground truth and measure exploitation explicitly. Neither prior work reports that predicted-vs-true return gap.

Baselines: DORL, a CQL- or IQL-style discrete offline RL method, SQN, and a greedy bandit should all be included.

Venue corrections relative to the earlier draft: KuaiSim is NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks; Virtual-Taobao is AAAI 2019; Deffayet et al. is SIGIR Forum 56(2), Dec 2022; the Chen et al. offline-RL survey is ACM TOIS 42(6), 2024.

topic: Offline-to-online (O2O) RL fine-tuning: the initial performance drop ("unlearning"/"policy collapse") and methods to mitigate it

papers.title: AWAC: Accelerating Online Reinforcement Learning with Offline Datasets
papers.authors: Ashvin Nair, Abhishek Gupta, Murtaza Dalal, Sergey Levine
papers.venue: arXiv preprint 2006.09359 (no conference venue listed on arXiv)
papers.summary: Actor-critic method where the critic is learned off-policy by TD and the actor is updated by advantage-weighted maximum likelihood, an implicit KL constraint toward the data/replay policy. The same objective is used offline and online, with offline data kept in the replay buffer.
papers.relevance: Canonical 'same objective in both phases' baseline. The advantage-weighted actor extends directly to a softmax policy over discrete items, so it is a cheap O2O baseline. Its constraint is global, toward the replay buffer. Our method instead modulates the constraint per (s,a) by logged support.

papers.title: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning via Balanced Replay and Pessimistic Q-Ensemble
papers.authors: Seunghyun Lee, Younggyo Seo, Kimin Lee, Pieter Abbeel, Jinwoo Shin
papers.summary: Identifies state-action distribution shift and bootstrap error on unfamiliar actions as the cause of collapse early in fine-tuning. Pretrains an ensemble of pessimistic (CQL) Q-functions offline. Fine-tunes with a balanced replay that prioritizes online samples plus near-on-policy offline samples, using a learned density-ratio estimate.
papers.relevance: Closest ancestor to 'dynamically mixing offline/online replay' combined with ensemble pessimism. Our support-aware variant can replace its learned density ratio with the KNOWN behavior propensity from our simulator, giving an exact support measure. It is a must-run ablation for the replay-composition question.
papers.correction_note: arXiv comments say 'CoRL 2021'. Authors match, with the first two contributing equally.

papers.title: Cal-QL: Calibrated Offline RL Pre-Training for Efficient Online Fine-Tuning
papers.authors: Mitsuhiko Nakamoto, Yuexiang Zhai, Anikait Singh, Max Sobol Mark, Yi Ma, Chelsea Finn, Aviral Kumar, Sergey Levine
papers.summary: Argues that CQL's over-underestimation makes Q-values mis-scaled. Early online samples of exploratory actions then look relatively better, which erodes the pretrained policy (the 'unlearning' dip). Cal-QL lower-bounds the conservative push-down by a reference policy's value (e.g., Monte-Carlo return of the behavior policy), a one-line change to CQL, so values stay conservative but calibrated.
papers.relevance: Directly applicable to discrete CQL: the logsumexp push-down is clipped at a reference value, and we have true behavior returns from the simulator to serve as that reference. It is the primary 'calibration' baseline for our claim that support-aware conservatism beats uniform calibrated conservatism on low-support items.
papers.correction_note: arXiv says 'Accepted to NeurIPS 2023'. Authors match. The abstract confirms the one-line CQL change and calibration against a reference policy.

papers.title: Policy Expansion for Bridging Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Haichao Zhang, Wei Xu, Haonan Yu
papers.summary: Freezes the offline policy as one member of a policy set and adds a new learnable policy. At each step it selects between their proposed actions with a softmax over critic values, so offline behavior is preserved early while new behavior is learned. The offline critic is transferred and keeps training online.
papers.relevance: A structural alternative to regularization that avoids destroying the offline policy. It applies to discrete actions, since we can compose the item proposals of two policies via Q. We differ by gating per action support rather than per policy.
papers.correction_note: The second author is Wei Xu, not 'We Xu'. The arXiv metadata carries the 'We Xu' typo, but DBLP and the ICLR listing give Wei Xu. The paper text (ar5iv) confirms that the offline critic is transferred and that a softmax over Q picks among the policies' proposals.

papers.authors: Philip J. Ball, Laura Smith, Ilya Kostrikov, Sergey Levine
papers.summary: RLPD: off-policy SAC with no offline pretraining. Each batch is 50/50 offline and online data (symmetric sampling), with LayerNorm in the critic to curb extrapolation, large ensembles, and a high update-to-data ratio.
papers.relevance: Strong 'no-pretraining' baseline and the reference point for replay ratio. Its symmetric sampling and LayerNorm critic carry over to discrete DQN-style critics. We test whether support-weighted sampling beats a fixed 50/50 mix.

Proves statistical and computational efficiency under bilinear rank when offline data covers a good policy, without initial-state coverage assumptions. Experiments include combination-lock tasks and hard-exploration Atari games such as Montezuma's Revenge.

papers.authors: Ikechukwu Uchendu, Ted Xiao, Yao Lu, Banghua Zhu, Mengyuan Yan, Joséphine Simon, Matthew Bennice, Chuyuan Fu, Cong Ma, Jiantao Jiao, Sergey Levine, Karol Hausman

papers.authors: Jianxiong Li, Xiao Hu, Haoran Xu, Jingjing Liu, Xianyuan Zhan, Ya-Qin Zhang

topic_notes:
CAUSES OF THE FINE-TUNING DROP. The literature names four interacting causes.

(1) Q-value miscalibration inherited from pessimism. CQL-style critics push down out-of-distribution (OOD) Q-values by an arbitrary amount. When online data arrives, an exploratory action's backed-up value can exceed the artificially low values of the pretrained policy's actions, so the actor 'unlearns'. Cal-QL is built on this argument. SO2 (biased estimates and wrong Q-ranking) and OPT (inaccurate offline value estimates) make related ones.

(2) State-action distribution shift. New online (s,a) pairs bootstrap from OOD actions at unfamiliar states, inflating TD error (Lee et al. 2021, ACA).

(3) Replay composition and update-to-data (UTD) ratio. Dropping offline data abruptly causes Q divergence at the switch (WSRL), and keeping too much slows improvement. UTD is a separate stability knob. RLPD runs a high UTD stably by adding LayerNorm and large ensembles. SUF stabilizes unconstrained fine-tuning by modifying the UTD ratio, reportedly a higher critic UTD with a lower actor UTD (a secondary source; the direction is not stated in SUF's abstract). Neither paper claims that high UTD by itself amplifies the collapse.

(4) Objective switch. Moving from an offline loss to a different online loss (e.g., CQL to SAC, or IQL to PPO) changes the fixed point. Uni-O4, AWAC, IQL and O3F keep one objective across phases for this reason.

Optimizer state is almost never ablated. Most implementations implicitly carry Adam moments over or silently re-create the optimizer. We should treat 'reset vs keep Adam state' and 'reset vs keep target network' as explicit ablations, and report them as such rather than as a literature claim.

MECHANISMS THAT CONTROL IT:
(a) Calibrated conservatism: Cal-QL clips the CQL push-down at a reference value.
(b) Conservatism or constraint annealing: PROTO uses a KL toward the previous (Polyak-averaged) iterate whose weight decays linearly to 0. Adaptive BC tunes the BC weight from performance feedback. ENOTO relaxes ensemble pessimism.
(c) State-adaptive balance: FamO2O.
(d) Data-source-dependent pessimism: APL is pessimistic on offline samples and optimistic on online ones.
(e) Ensembles and uncertainty: Lee et al. 2021, ENOTO, BOORL (probability matching from Chongjie Zhang's group), Adaptive BC with REDQ.
(f) Replay design: Lee et al. use density-ratio balanced replay. RLPD samples 50/50 symmetrically. WSRL discards offline data after a policy-rollout warm-up. SUF adjusts the UTD ratio.
(g) Structural preservation: PEX freezes the offline policy and adds a new one, choosing between their actions with a softmax over Q. JSRL uses the offline policy as a roll-in guide.
(h) Critic surgery at the switch: ACA re-aligns the critic, and OPT trains a new critic.
Li et al. ('The Three Regimes of O2O RL', arXiv 2510.01460, an oral at an ICML 2026 workshop, not the main conference) argue that the right stability knob depends on whether the pretrained policy or the dataset is the stronger asset. Their predictions matched 45 of 63 cases, with 3 opposite mismatches.

INHERITANCE.
- Actor and critic weights are copied by AWAC, IQL, Cal-QL, Lee et al., PROTO, ENOTO and FamO2O.
- PEX keeps the offline actor frozen as a set member and transfers the offline critic, which keeps training (confirmed in the paper text).
- ACA modifies the critic before fine-tuning. OPT adds a freshly trained critic alongside the inherited one.
- RLPD and Hy-Q start from scratch, using offline data only through the buffer.
- Replay buffers: Cal-QL, IQL, AWAC and RLPD keep offline data, mixed with online data. Lee et al. reweight it. WSRL drops it.
- Target networks are typically copied with the critic. Optimizer state is rarely discussed.

DISCRETE-ACTION APPLICABILITY. Most methods were benchmarked on continuous D4RL, but several port cleanly to a categorical item policy:
- Discrete CQL (exact logsumexp over items) and Cal-QL.
- Q-ensembles (REM or multi-head) for ENOTO/BOORL-style gating.
- APL value-based variants.
- AWAC/IQL advantage-weighted softmax policies.
- PROTO and Adaptive BC, with the KL or cross-entropy computed exactly over items.
- PEX policy-set selection via Q.
- Hy-Q (DQN-based), RLPD sampling, and WSRL warm-up.

SO2's target-action noise and Uni-O4's Gaussian-policy specifics need re-design. Reincarnating RL (Atari) and DRIFT (macro-action MinAtar with 6^K actions, Jericho, candidate sets) are the main discrete O2O evidence. DRIFT runs Cal-QL and IQL as discrete O2O baselines; a plain CQL baseline was not confirmed. Reincarnating RL (Agarwal, Schwarzer, Castro, Courville, Bellemare) reports that fine-tuning CQL-pretrained agents degrades with 1-step returns, and more so with higher CQL coefficients (its Fig. A.13).

IMPLICATION FOR US. The gap is per-(s,a) modulation using KNOWN behavior propensities. FamO2O adapts per state with a learned balance. Lee et al. use a learned density ratio. ENOTO and BOORL use global or ensemble-driven relaxation.
